items.abstract: <jats:p>Current evaluation paradigms for agentic AI focus predominantly on task success rates under nominal conditions, creating a critical blind spot: agents may succeed under ideal circumstances while exhibiting catastrophic failure modes under stress. We propose HB-Eval, a rigorous methodology for measuring behavioral reliability through three complementary metrics: Failure Resilience Rate (FRR) quantifying recovery from systematic fault injection, Planning Efficiency Index (PEI) measuring trajectory optimality against oracle-verified paths, and Traceability Index (TI) evaluating reasoning transparency via calibrated LLM-as-a-Judge (κ = 0.82 with human consensus). Through systematic evaluation across 500 episodes spanning three strategically selected domains (logistics, healthcare, coding), we demonstrate a 42.9 percentage point reliability gap between nominal success rates and stressed performance for baseline architectures. We introduce an integrated resilience architecture combining Eval-Driven Memory (EDM) for selective experience consolidation, Adaptive Planning for PEI-guided recovery, and Human-Centered Explainability (HCI-EDM) for trust calibration. This closed-loop system achieves 94.2% ±2.1% FRR with statistically significant improvements over base lines (Cohen’s d = 3.28, p &lt; 0.001), establishing a rigorous methodology for transitioning agentic AI from capability demonstrations to reliability-certified deployment. We conclude by proposing a three-tier certification framework and identifying critical research directions for community validation.</jats:p>
title: HB-Eval: A System-Level Reliability Evaluation and Certification Framework for Agentic AI
Beyond Task Completion: An Assessment Framework for Evaluating Agentic AI Systems

items.abstract:
<jats:p>Background:  Complexity ideas originating in mathematics and the natural sciences have begun to inform evaluation practice. A new wave in evaluation history is about to break. A new mindset, new methods, and new evaluation processes are being summoned to explore and address the challenges of global pandemics, growing inequities, and existential environmental risks. This is part of a broader paradigm shift underway in science where interdisciplinarity has become the norm rather than the exception.
Purpose: This article explores the utility of a complexity framework for a more effective evaluation function. It unearths the antecedents of complexity thinking; explores its relevance to evolving knowledge paradigms; provides a bird’s eye view of complexity concepts; uses the logic of complex adaptive systems to unpack the role of evaluation in society; and draws the implications of contemporary social challenges for evaluation policy directions.
Setting: Not applicable.
Intervention: Not applicable.
Research design: Not applicable.
Findings: The evaluation complexity challenge coincides with an urgent imperative: social transformation. The on-going pandemic has brought to light the disproportionate effects of health emergencies on disadvantaged groups and emphasized the urgency of improving the interface between humans and nature. It has also demonstrated the importance of modelling for policy making – as well as its limitations. Evaluation, a complex adaptive system, should be transformed to serve society.
Keywords: complexity; computers; disciplines; emergence; modelling; paradigm, systems</jats:p>
title: Towards a Complexity Framework for Transformative Evaluation

items.abstract: <jats:p>Traditional approaches to network management have been accessible only to a handful of highly-trained network operators with significant expert knowledge. This creates barriers for lay users to easily manage their networks without resorting to experts. With recent development of powerful large language models (LLMs) for language comprehension, we design a system to make network management accessible to a broader audience of non-experts by allowing users to converse with networks in natural language. To e!ectively leverage advancements in LLMs, we propose an agentic framework that uses an intermediate representation to streamline configuration across diverse vendor equipment, retrieves the network state from memory in real-time, and provides an interface for external feedback. We also conduct pilot studies to collect real user data of natural language utterances for network control, and present a visualization interface to facilitate dialogue-driven user interaction and enable large-scale data collection for future development. Preliminary experiments validate the e!ectiveness of our proposed system components with LLM integration on both synthetic and real user utterances. Through our data collection and visualization e!orts, we pave the way for more e!ective use of LLMs and democratize network control for everyday users.1</jats:p>
title: An LLM-based Agentic Framework for Accessible NetworkControl

items.abstract: <jats:p>Contemporary agentic AI systems face critical challenges in tool orchestration, dynamic coordination, and framework interoperability. I present FATA (Framework Agnostic and Task Agnostic Agentic AI), a novel control plane design pattern that enables scalable, distributed multi-agent orchestration through serverless architecture. FATA introduces a unified tool management layer that dynamically routes, validates, and governs tool interactions while maintaining framework independence. My approach distinguishes between specialized AI agents for targeted automation and collaborative agentic ecosystems with emergent collective intelligence. Through systematic evaluation across cybersecurity, compliance, and document processing domains, FATA demonstrates the capability to reduce developer complexity, enable runtime adaptability, and provide robust governance mechanisms for enterprise-scale agentic deployments.</jats:p>
title: FATA: A Framework-Agnostic, Task-Agnostic Agentic AI Platform for Serverless Multi-Agent Orchestration

items.abstract:
<jats:p>Abstract:
Adaptive public policy increasingly depends on evidence that is incomplete, heterogeneous, time-varying and institutionally constrained. This monograph develops an integrated framework for matrix-completion evaluation, dynamic policy learning and agentic decision systems capable of supporting public decisions without collapsing statistical uncertainty, social equity or administrative accountability into a single optimization objective. The framework links sparse-policy data reconstruction with causal inference, distributional evaluation, sequential decision theory, constrained reinforcement learning, trustworthy artificial intelligence, policy-as-code and reproducible MLOps. Matrix completion is positioned as an evaluation instrument for missing jurisdiction-by-outcome structures; dynamic learning is formulated as controlled adaptation under budget, legal, service and equity constraints; and agentic systems are designed as permissioned, auditable workflows with human review and traceable evidence. Five chapters progress from foundations and uncertainty through causal modelling, machine learning, scalable data engineering and cross-sector policy applications. The analysis emphasizes global transfer across South Asia, Europe, Africa and the Americas while recognizing differences in data capacity, institutional authority and regulatory expectations. Research outputs include evaluation designs, mathematical formulations, decision metrics, assurance protocols, governance artifacts and deployment architectures intended for researchers, public agencies, regulated industries and policy laboratories.
Keywords
adaptive public policy intelligence, matrix completion, policy evaluation, causal inference, heterogeneous treatment effects, dynamic policy learning, reinforcement learning, approximate dynamic programming, agentic AI, multi-agent systems, public administration, algorithmic accountability, trustworthy AI, policy-as-code, MLOps, public-sector data, distributional evaluation, social equity, regulatory intelligence, scenario analysis, uncertainty quantification, digital governance, comparative policy, institutional learning</jats:p>
title: Adaptive Public Policy Intelligence: Matrix-Completion Evaluation, Dynamic Policy Learning and Agentic Decision Systems

items.abstract: <jats:p>Recent research has introduced agentic artificial intelligence architectures for educational systems in which specialized AI agents coordinate conversational tutoring, curriculum generation, speech interaction, and safety governance. While such architectures promise improved personalization, instructional reliability, and scalable learning delivery, systematic evaluation frameworks for assessing the performance and governance characteristics of agentic learning systems remain limited. This research contributes an evaluation methodology for next-generation agentic AI learning environments, providing a foundation for measuring reliability, safety governance, and adaptive learning effectiveness in multi-agent educational systems.</jats:p>
